newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals -- Japan magnesium price seen rising.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals -- Japan magnesium price seen rising.

text.p: Magnesium prices are set to rise in Japan, after Norsk Hydro raised the European producer price just ahead of talks between Japanese traders and end-users on domestic third-quarter prices, traders said on Tuesday.

"The magnesium price is definitely heading upwards, although we can't pass higher international prices directly on to domestic users," said one trader. "The price of Chinese metal has already risen more than people had expected."

Traders said they hoped to raise the domestic magnesium price in talks next week with end-users on third-quarter deliveries, despite the dollar's recent fall against the yen. A weaker dollar against the yen makes Japan's imports cheaper.
A source close to Norsk Hydro said the Norwegian firm was also likely to press for a higher price in separate talks early next month on its third-quarter deliveries to Japan.
Norsk supplied more than 4,000 tonnes of pure magnesium to Japan last year, nearly 15 percent of the country's total magnesium demand, the source added.
Last week, Hydro Magnesium, Norsk Hydro's Brussels-based division, raised its European producer price for pure magnesium.
In the bismuth market, a trader in southern China said Chinese bismuth producers offered material at $3.80 a lb.
China produces about 1,400 tonnes of bismuth a year, industry sources said, versus annual global demand of about 5,500 tonnes.
Another source in China said containers of Chinese bismuth were available but were not being offered because holders of the minor metal expected prices to strengthen.
"There is no business yet at that level," he said.
"Quite a bit went to Europe when the prices started to rally about a month ago," he added.
In Japan, traders said bismuth was trading close to $4.00 per pound, reflecting rising prices overseas against the backdrop of low Peruvian and Mexican stocks.
"Domestic supply has dropped as some smelters have shut down their refineries," one trader said, referring to closure of zinc capacity by Nippon Mining and Metals Corp and Mitsubishi Materials Corp.

He said a shift in Japan towards recycled batteries rather than mine production as a source of lead has also added to upward price pressure on bismuth, a by-product of zinc and lead production that is used mainly by electronics companies here.
"Japan might become an importer of the metal in the future," another trader added.
Official statistics show that Japan consumed 558 tonnes of bismuth in 1995, versus production of 150 tonnes, making the country the world's fourth largest producer after Peru, Mexico and China.
Traders in Tokyo said the molybdenum price was holding firm at $4.60 per pound amid talks of lower production by Chile's Codelco, one of the metal's major producers.

"The price is quite high but it might be justified considering the latest bullish factors, including Codelco's lower output and strong demand from pipe producers and shipmakers," said one trader at a major trading house.

Another trader said he expected the price to edge up towards five dollars, as some market participants now doubted additional supply from U.S. Molycorp would be sufficient to ease the current tightness.
"It might not go as high as five dollars, but people are turning bullish again and dealers are reluctant to sell the metal at the moment," the trader said.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai newsroom +86-21-6279-8544. -- Nao Nakanishi, Tokyo commodities desk +81-3-3432-7431
